[[File:Echium pininanaWEB.jpg|thumb|Echium pininana, Tree Echium.]]
'''''Echium pininana''''', [[Common name|commonly known]] as the '''tree echium''', '''pine echium''', '''giant viper's-bugloss''', or '''tower of jewels''',<ref name=":6" /><ref name="RHSPF">{{cite web|title=RHS Plantfinder - ''Echium pininata''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/6295/i-Echium-pininana-i/Details|access-date=12 January 2018}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the borage family [[Boraginaceae]]. It is [[Endemism|endemic]] to the [[Canary Islands]], where it is restricted to the island of [[La Palma]].<ref name=canar>Manuel Arechavaleta, S. Rodríguez, Nieves Zurita, A. García (Hrsg.): ''[http://www.gobiernodecanarias.org/medioambiente/piac/descargas/Biodiversidad/Listas-Especies/Lista_Especies_Silvestres.pdf Lista de especies silvestres de Canarias. Hongos, plantas y animales terrestres]'' (''List of Forest Species of the Canary Islands''). 2009. Gobierno de Canarias, p. 151 {{ISBN|978-84-89729-21-6}}</ref> ''Echium pininana'' is an [[Endangered species (IUCN status)|endangered species]],<ref name="IUCN"/> and is listed in Appendix I to, and is therefore protected under, the [[Berne Convention on the Conservation of European Wildlife and Natural Habitats|Convention on the Conservation of European Wildlife and Natural Habitats]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Echium pininana - Webb. & Berth.|url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/species/15781|url-status=live|access-date=2021-06-19|website=eunis.eea.europa.eu|publisher=European Environment Agency|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140422234415/http://eunis.eea.europa.eu/species/15781 |archive-date=2014-04-22 }}</ref> The [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''pininana'' is [[Latin]] for "small pine",<ref name="RHSLG">{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for Gardeners|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|year=2012|isbn=978-1845337315|location=United Kingdom}}</ref> though ''E. pininana'' is neither closely related to the [[pine]], nor does it resemble that plant.

== Description ==

=== Lifecycle ===
''Echium pininana'' is [[biennial plant|biennial]] or triennial,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Echium pininana|url=https://www.gardenersworld.com/plants/echium-pininana/|access-date=2021-06-19|website=BBC Gardeners' World Magazine|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> meaning each plant lives for only two or three years respectively. It is a [[monocarpic]] species;<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Al-Shehbaz|first=Ihsan A.|title=The Genera of Boraginaceae in the Southeastern United States |date=1991|journal=Journal of the Arnold Arboretum. Supplementary Series|volume=1|pages=1–169|doi=10.5962/p.315943 |jstor=43782784 |issn=2472-8659|doi-access=free}}</ref> each plant flowers only once before dying.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020|title=Definition of monocarpic|url=https://www.lexico.com/definition/monocarpic|url-status=dead|access-date=2021-06-18|website=Lexico.com|publisher=Oxford University Press|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210624201208/https://www.lexico.com/definition/monocarpic |archive-date=2021-06-24 }}</ref>

=== Morphology ===
In their first year, plants produce a [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]] of [[Glossary of leaf morphology|lanceolate leaves]] approximately {{Convert|7|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} in length, with silver hairs.<ref name="RHSPF" /> Plants also produce a [[Trunk (botany)|trunk]] {{Convert|3-8|ft|m|1|order=flip|abbr=on}} tall in their first year,<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|title=Echium pininana 'Blue Steeple'|url=https://www.chicagobotanic.org/plantcollections/plantfinder/echium_pininana_blue_steeple--blue_steeple_tower_jewels|url-status=live|access-date=2021-06-19|website=www.chicagobotanic.org|publisher=Chicago Botanic Garden|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210624203818/https://www.chicagobotanic.org/plantcollections/plantfinder/echium_pininana_blue_steeple--blue_steeple_tower_jewels |archive-date=2021-06-24 }}</ref> which is covered with many lanceolate leaves.<ref name=":2" /> In their second (or third) year, plants produce a [[Conifer cone|cone]]-like [[inflorescence]] up to {{convert|4|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} high with a dense mass of leaves and small blue [[flower]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Carlquist|first=Sherwin|date=1970|title=Wood Anatomy of Echium (Boraginaceae)|url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/84114066.pdf|journal=Aliso: A Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Botany|volume=7|issue=2|via=CORE}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=Kelley|first=Ronald B.|date=2012|title=Echium pininana, in Jepson Flora Project (eds.)|url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=77364|url-status=live|access-date=2021-06-19|website=Jepson eFlora|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170829060005/http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=77364 |archive-date=2017-08-29 }}</ref> Between April and June, the flower spike can grow {{convert|5|cm|in|abbr=on|0}} per day.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Robinson|first=David|date=2003|title=Plants that changed my life|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/45142512|journal=The Horticulturist|volume=12|issue=4|pages=5–9|jstor=45142512 |issn=0964-8992}}</ref> Flowers are funnel-shaped,<ref>{{Cite web|title=BBC - Gardening: Plant Finder - Tree echium|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/gardening/plants/plant_finder/plant_pages/11031.shtml|access-date=2021-06-19|website=www.bbc.co.uk}}</ref> and each produce up to 1.4 [[Litre#SI prefixes applied to the litre|μL]] of [[nectar]], which is approximately 26% [[sugar]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Valido|first1=Alfredo|last2=Dupont|first2=Yoko L.|last3=Olesen|first3=Jens M.|date=2004|title=Bird-Flower Interactions in the Macaronesian Islands|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3554673|journal=Journal of Biogeography|volume=31|issue=12|pages=1945–1953|doi=10.1111/j.1365-2699.2004.01116.x |jstor=3554673 |hdl=10261/63423 |s2cid=35788157 |issn=0305-0270|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Flowers at the bottom of the flower spike are first to open, with those at the top opening last.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Woodley|first=Millie|date=11 January 2021|title=Plant of the month|url=https://www.fulhampalace.org/news/plant-of-the-month-january-2021/|url-status=live|access-date=2021-06-19|website=Fulham Palace|publisher=Fulham Palace Trust|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210111111625/https://www.fulhampalace.org/news/plant-of-the-month-january-2021/ |archive-date=2021-01-11 }}</ref> [[Pollinator|Pollinators]] such as [[Bee|bees]], [[Butterfly|butterflies]], and [[Moth|moths]] are attracted to the flowers.<ref name=":0" /> Following [[pollination]], each flower produces four [[Nut (fruit)|nutlets]].<ref name=":5" /> Each plant can produce over 200,000 [[Seed|seeds]],<ref name=":1" /> which are [[Seed dispersal|disbursed]] short distances by the wind.<ref name=":5">{{Cite Government|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190326151111/http://vro.agriculture.vic.gov.au/dpi/vro/vrosite.nsf/pages/weeds_giant-vipers-bugloss |archive-date=2019-03-26 }}</ref> 

=== Phytochemistry ===
Various [[Pyrrolizidine alkaloid|pyrrolizidine alkaloids]], a class of [[Toxicity|toxic]] [[Organic compound|organic compounds]] that may cause liver damage,<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020|title=Definition of pyrrolizidine alkaloid|url=https://www.lexico.com/definition/pyrrolizidine_alkaloid|url-status=dead|access-date=2021-06-19|website=Lexico.com|publisher=Oxford University Press|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210624201205/https://www.lexico.com/definition/pyrrolizidine_alkaloid |archive-date=2021-06-24 }}</ref> have been isolated from ''Echium pininana.''<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Roeder|first1=E.|last2=Liu|first2=K.|last3=Bourauel|first3=T.|date=1991-01-01|title=Pyrrolizidine alkaloids from Echium pininana|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0031942200982633|journal=Phytochemistry|language=en|volume=30|issue=9|pages=3107–3110|doi=10.1016/S0031-9422(00)98263-3|issn=0031-9422|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The plant is toxic to [[Horse|horses]].<ref name=":0" />

== Phylogeny ==
''Echium pininana'', ''[[Echium simplex|E. simplex]]'', and ''[[Echium wildpretii|E. wildpretii]]'' comprise a [[Monophyly|monophyletic clade]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last=Bramwell|first=David|date=1973|title=Studies in the genus Echium from Macaronesia|url=https://mdc.ulpgc.es/utils/getfile/collection/MDC/id/41256/filename/74846.PDF|journal=Monographiae Biologicae Canarienses|volume=4|pages=71–82}}</ref> All three of these ''Echium'' species are monocarpic, have a similar [[Habit (biology)|habit]], similar floral morphology, and produce a dimethylated [[Flavones|flavone]] not detected in other ''Echium'' species.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" />  

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Echium pininana'' is endemic to the island of La Palma in the Canary Islands, where it grows in [[laurel forest]]s.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|last=Wilson|first=Matthew|date=4 March 2016|title=Rocket plant takes off: how towering Echium pininana has spread|url=https://www.ft.com/content/d87018b8-dbaa-11e5-a72f-1e7744c66818|url-status=live|access-date=2021-06-18|website=FT.com|publisher=Financial Times|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190924075942/https://www.ft.com/content/d87018b8-dbaa-11e5-a72f-1e7744c66818 |archive-date=2019-09-24 }}</ref> It is endangered due to habitat loss caused by [[agriculture]].<ref name=":1" /> Outside La Palma, ''Echium pininana'' has been introduced to [[France]], [[Great Britain]], [[Ireland]], [[New Zealand]] (both [[North Island|North]] and [[South Island]]), and the [[United States]] (north and central coast of [[California]]).<ref name="POWO">{{Cite web|title=Echium pininana Webb & Berthel.|url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:115832-1|url-status=live|access-date=2021-06-19|website=Plants of the World Online|publisher=Kew Science|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120041837/http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:115832-1 |archive-date=2021-01-20 }}</ref><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Echium pininana Webb & Berthel.|url=https://www.gbif.org/species/4068166|access-date=2021-06-19|website=www.gbif.org|language=en}}</ref> It is also in [[Ex situ conservation|''ex situ'' conservation]]; in fact, the ''ex situ'' conservation population is greater than the wild population.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Maunder|first1=Mike|last2=Higgens|first2=Sarah|date=1998|title=A Survey of Bern Convention Plant Taxa in European Botanic Gardens - initial findings and implications|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24753901|journal=Botanic Gardens Conservation News|volume=2|issue=10|pages=29–31|jstor=24753901 |issn=0965-2582}}</ref> It is conserved in [[Botanical garden|botanical gardens]] such as [[Kew Gardens]] in [[London]], where it has [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]].<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2009|editor-last=Verdcourt|editor-first=B.|title=Additions to the Wild Fauna and Flora of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/20649641|journal=Kew Bulletin|volume=64|issue=1|pages=183–194|jstor=20649641 |issn=0075-5974|last1=Verdcourt |first1=B. |doi=10.1007/s12225-008-9084-0 |s2cid=40246634 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
''Echium pininana'' is cultivated as a [[Ornamental plant|garden ornamental]], and has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name="RHSPF" /><ref>{{cite web|date=July 2017|title=AGM Plants - Ornamental|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf|access-date=24 January 2018|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|page=35}}</ref> It is used as a [[Bedding (horticulture)|bedding plant]] or planted in [[Herbaceous border|borders]], and grows best in full sun.<ref name=":7" /> It is recommended for the southern maritime counties of [[England]], the [[Channel Islands]] and the [[Scilly Isles]]. There are, however, reports of successful cultivation in the [[English Midlands]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.expressandstar.com/news/local-hubs/staffordshire/cannock-chase/2017/06/02/is-this-cannock-plant-the-tallest-in-the-country/ |date=2017-06-02 |accessdate=2021-07-30 |title=Is this Cannock plant the tallest in the country? |author=Joe Edwards |newspaper=Express & Star}}</ref> and [[Yorkshire]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.alamy.com/giant-vipers-bugloss-tree-echium-pine-echium-echium-pininana-east-yorkshire-england-uk-gb-image363826142.html |title= Giant Viper's bugloss, Tree Echium, Pine echium, Echium pininana. East Yorkshire, England, UK, GB. - Image ID: 2C3WKXP |website=www.alamy.com |accessdate=2021-07-30 |date=2020-05-25 |author=Alan Mather}}</ref> albeit in favourable locations. Specimens are also grown in [[Dublin]] gardens at [[Howth]] and in the [[Irish National Botanic Gardens]] at [[Glasnevin]]. The plant also grows readily in [[North Wales]] where it seeds very widely. Although ''E. pininana'' is [[half-hardy]] in Britain and Ireland, it will self-seed to form clusters of plants, and it is suggested that by [[natural selection]] a hardier variety will emerge.<ref name=":1">{{cite web | url = http://www.earlscliffe.com/echium_pininana.htm | title = Increase Of Cold Hardiness Of Echium Pininana Through Natural Selection | date = December 1992 | access-date = 22 May 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090627042817/http://www.earlscliffe.com/echium_pininana.htm | archive-date = 27 June 2009 | url-status = dead }}</ref> The plant is most vulnerable to frosts in its first year. Because of its large leaves when partly grown, it is also very susceptible to wind damage. Hence a sheltered garden position is essential. ''Echium pininana'' 'Alba' is a [[cultivar]] with white flowers.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Fallon|first=Fionnuala|date=2021-06-12|title=Ten summer flowers to add height and energy to your garden|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/life-and-style/homes-and-property/gardens/ten-summer-flowers-to-add-height-and-energy-to-your-garden-1.4583323|url-status=live|access-date=2021-06-19|newspaper=The Irish Times|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210613183610/https://www.irishtimes.com/life-and-style/homes-and-property/gardens/ten-summer-flowers-to-add-height-and-energy-to-your-garden-1.4583323 |archive-date=2021-06-13 }}</ref>
